overview.title: Student & Teacher Overview: Lesson 11
overview.text: In this lesson, you will contrast the solution sets of equations (typically discrete points) with inequalities (continuous rays or segments). You will learn standard conventions for number line graphing: open circles for strict inequalities ($<, >$) and closed solid dots for inclusive inequalities ($\le, \ge$).
outcomes: Understand that the solution set of an inequality often contains infinitely many real numbers.
Accurately graph solution sets on a real coordinate line using rays and boundary points.
Use open circles for non-included boundary values ($<, >$) and solid closed dots for included values ($\le, \ge$).
overview.teacherInsight: Make sure students test points on either side of the boundary to verify their shaded direction. For example, to check $x > 3$, test $x = 0$ (False, not shaded) and $x = 5$ (True, shaded).

vocabulary.definition: A mathematical statement comparing two expressions using relation symbols <, ≤, >, or ≥.
A hollow dot on a number line representing an exclusive boundary that is not included in the solution set (< or >).
A solid filled dot on a number line representing an inclusive boundary that is included in the solution set (≤ or ≥).
A continuous portion of the coordinate line extending indefinitely in one direction from an endpoint.

practiceQuestions.question: A number line graph displays a solid closed circle at $2$ with shading extending continuously to the left toward $-\infty$. What is the correct description in words and formal set notation?
options: The set of all real numbers less than or equal to $2$; $\{r \text{ real} \mid r \le 2\}$
The set of all real numbers strictly less than $2$; $\{r \text{ real} \mid r < 2\}$
The set of all integers greater than or equal to $2$; $\{r \in \mathbb{Z} \mid r \ge 2\}$
practiceQuestions.explanation: From the official Eureka Math Exit Ticket Key: A solid circle at 2 indicates inclusion ($r \le 2$). In set notation: $\{r \text{ real} \mid r \le 2\}$.

practiceQuestions.question: Which of the following equations is guaranteed to have a solution set of all real numbers?
options: $x + 2 = 2 + x$, because both sides are algebraically equivalent by the commutative property of addition.
$3x + 1 = 3x + 4$, because subtracting $3x$ leaves a valid inequality.
$x^2 = 4$, because both sides contain positive constants.
$\frac{x}{x} = 1$, because any number divided by itself is 1.
practiceQuestions.explanation: By the commutative property of addition, $x + 2$ is identically equal to $2 + x$ for every real number $x$, so the solution set is all real numbers.

exitTicket.title: Lesson 11 Exit Ticket: Solution Sets for Equations and Inequalities
exitTicket.prompt: Here is the graphical representation of a set of real numbers: A solid ray extending to the left from 2 on the number line. Describe this set in words, set notation, and write an inequality that has this solution set. Indicate whether 3x + 1 = 3x + 1 and x + 2 = 2 + x have a solution set of all real numbers.
exitTicket.solution: In words: The set of all real numbers less than or equal to two. In set notation: {r real | r <= 2}. Inequality: w - 7 <= -5 (or simply r <= 2). For 3x + 1 = 3x + 1: Yes, the solution set is all real numbers (identity). For x + 2 = 2 + x: Yes, algebraically equivalent by commutative property, solution set is all real numbers.

guidedExercises.title: Example 1: Graphing Solution Sets of Inequalities on a Number Line
guidedExercises.problem: Solve $3x - 5 \le 10$ and express the solution set in three mathematical forms: inequality notation, set-builder notation, and interval notation. Graph the solution on a real number line.
guidedExercises.scaffolding: Use the addition and multiplication properties of inequality. Distinguish between strict ($<$) and non-strict ($\le$) boundaries.

steps.label: Isolate the variable term
steps.explanation: Add 5 to both sides using the addition property of inequality.

steps.label: Solve for $x$
steps.explanation: Divide both sides by positive 3; the inequality direction remains unchanged.

steps.label: Express in standard mathematical notations
steps.explanation: Use a solid bracket ']' because $5$ is included.

guidedExercises.finalAnswer: x \le 5; \quad \{x \in \mathbb{R} \mid x \le 5\}; \quad (-\infty, 5] \quad \text{(Closed circle at 5, arrow extending left)}
guidedExercises.commonPitfall: Using an open circle at $5$. Remember: $\le$ and $\ge$ include the boundary point and require a solid filled circle and square bracket '[' or ']'. $<$ and $>$ exclude the boundary and require an open circle and parenthesis '(' or ')'.

problemSet.title: Official Worksheet: Problem Set & Practice
problemSet.description: Express solution sets of inequalities using words, formal set notation, and number-line graphs.

problems.prompt:
For each solution set graphed below, describe the set in words, write it in formal set notation, and provide an inequality:
(a) Open circle at -4, shaded to the right.
(b) Solid circle at 7, shaded to the left.
problems.solution:
(a) Words: All real numbers strictly greater than -4. Set notation: {x \text{ real} \mid x > -4}. Inequality: x > -4.
(b) Words: All real numbers less than or equal to 7. Set notation: {x \text{ real} \mid x \le 7}. Inequality: x \le 7.

problems.prompt: Explain the difference in meaning between an open circle and a closed circle on a number line graph.
problems.solution: An open circle indicates a strict boundary value that is excluded from the solution set (< or >), whereas a closed (solid) circle indicates that the boundary endpoint itself satisfies the inequality and is included (\le or \ge).
